developer_request: I do not understand this codebase. I built it with AI over time and it may be very messy. Do not make me diagnose it; preserve what is valuable, recover what is real, and take responsibility for moving it forward.
known_facts: The repository may contain duplicated implementations, stale documents, abandoned branches, weak tests, generated code, or contradictory architecture left by prior AI-assisted development.
The owner cannot reliably judge code quality or architecture but may know which real user behaviors, workflows, language, data, external commitments, and product outcomes matter.
Some apparently ugly implementation may encode already validated behavior or compatibility constraints.
A rewrite would be easy to propose before the system has reconstructed what value and evidence already exist.
expected_first_moves: preserve the current repository and recover the smallest trustworthy picture of actual behavior, current users or acceptance paths, deployment/runtime facts, tests, contracts, data shapes, and active work topology
separate accidental technical debt from product behavior, domain rules, user evidence, external compatibility, and other value that should survive any repair
treat the owner's non-technical product/domain statements as evidence in their proper scope instead of asking them to explain the code
prefer a bounded repair or salvage path when it can prove the next outcome; consider replacement or rewrite only after evidence shows salvage is materially worse for outcome, risk, or reversibility
recompute the project frontier after each verified repair rather than stopping at a repository audit
must_preserve: working behavior that has real acceptance or usage evidence even when its implementation is unattractive
domain/product intent that the owner can establish without technical vocabulary
historical conflicts and unknowns until current authority justifies a resolution
must_not: treat messy code as permission for a whole-repository rewrite
ask the owner to choose architecture or explain technical internals they cannot know
delete historical or production-relevant behavior merely to make the codebase look coherent
stop after producing a cleanup plan while a safe executable project frontier remains
lessons: Brownfield rescue begins by recovering value, not by judging code aesthetics.
A non-technical owner can delegate engineering while retaining authority over product/domain truth they actually know.
Rewrite is an evidence-backed option, not the default emotional reaction to technical mess.
